title: Malta Year 8 Math — All 19 Chapters: Basic Set A
question: Set A: one quick step from each of the nineteen chapters, with new numbers.
intro: **Set A:** the same 38 steps as Basic, new questions, two per chapter.

questions.title: Ch 1 Directed Numbers · Car park lift
questions.prompt:
In a Valletta car park, floor 0 is the street.

Floor \(-2\) means 2 floors below the street.

A lift starts on floor \(-2\) and goes up 6 floors.

Which floor does it stop at?
questions.figure_alt: A building with floors −3 to 5 and street level at floor 0. A lift car is on floor −2 and an arrow goes up 6 floors to a floor marked with a question mark.
questions.solution:
Up means add:

\[-2 + 6 = \boxed{4}\]

\(-8\) moves 6 floors down instead of up.

questions.title: Ch 1 Directed Numbers · Colder freezer
questions.prompt:
A freezer is at \(-6\,^\circ\text{C}\) (6 degrees below zero).

You turn it down and it gets 8 degrees colder.

What is the temperature now?
questions.figure_alt: A freezer next to a thermometer from −16 to 4 °C. The start −6 is marked; an arrow goes 8 degrees down to a question mark.
questions.solution:
Colder means move **down** the thermometer:

\[-6 - 8 = \boxed{-14}\]

\(-2\) takes 6 from 8 and forgets that both moves go below zero.

questions.title: Ch 2 Number Work · Pastizzi boxes
questions.prompt:
A tray has 5 loose pastizzi and 3 boxes with 4 pastizzi in each box.

The total is \(5 + 3\times4\).

How many pastizzi are there?
questions.figure_alt: Five loose pastizzi plus three boxes with four pastizzi each, then equals a question mark.
questions.solution:
BIDMAS: multiply first (the boxes), then add.

\[3\times4 = 12\]

\[5 + 12 = \boxed{17}\]

\(32\) adds first, as if it were \((5 + 3)\times4\).

questions.title: Ch 2 Number Work · Square patio
questions.prompt:
A square patio is 7 tiles long and 7 tiles wide.

The number of tiles is \(7^2\) (the small 2 means 7 times itself).

How many tiles are there?
questions.figure_alt: A 7 by 7 square of tiles; how many tiles in all is the question.
questions.solution:
A square number is rows times columns:

\[7^2 = 7\times7\]

\[7\times7 = \boxed{49}\]

\(14\) is \(7\times2\), not \(7\times7\).

questions.title: Ch 3 Angles · Road junction
questions.prompt:
A side road meets a straight main road.

The two angles at the corner sit on a straight line.

One angle is \(72^\circ\).

Find the other angle.
questions.figure_alt: A straight main road with a side road leaving it. The right angle at the corner is 72°; the left angle is a question mark.
questions.solution:
Angles on a straight line add up to \(180^\circ\):

\[180^\circ - 72^\circ = \boxed{108^\circ}\]

\(288^\circ\) uses \(360^\circ\), which is for angles around a point.

questions.title: Ch 3 Angles · Luzzu sail
questions.prompt:
The sail of a luzzu (a Maltese fishing boat) is a triangle.

The mast and the bottom of the sail make a right angle (\(90^\circ\)).

Another corner is \(50^\circ\).

Find the top angle.
questions.figure_alt: A boat with a triangular sail. The corner at the bottom of the mast is a right angle, the far bottom corner is 50°, and the top angle is a question mark.
questions.solution:
The angles in a triangle add up to \(180^\circ\):

\[180^\circ - 90^\circ - 50^\circ = \boxed{40^\circ}\]

\(130^\circ\) forgets the right angle and takes only \(50^\circ\) from \(180^\circ\).

questions.title: Ch 4 Fractions · Birthday cake
questions.prompt:
A round cake is cut into 6 equal slices.

A fraction like \(\frac{1}{6}\) means 1 slice out of the 6.

You eat 2 slices and a friend eats 3 slices.

What fraction of the cake is eaten?
questions.figure_alt: A round cake in 6 slices: 2 orange slices (you), 3 green slices (a friend); the eaten fraction is a question mark.
questions.solution:
Same size slices, so add the tops:

\[\frac{2}{6} + \frac{3}{6} = \boxed{\frac{5}{6}}\]

\(\frac{5}{12}\) adds the bottoms too, but there are still 6 slices, not 12.

questions.title: Ch 4 Fractions · Cheese pastizzi
questions.prompt:
A tray holds 30 pastizzi.

\(\frac{2}{5}\) of them are cheese pastizzi (\(\frac{2}{5}\) means 2 out of every 5 equal parts).

How many cheese pastizzi are there?
questions.figure_alt: 30 pastizzi in 5 equal boxes of 6; 2 boxes are shaded and labelled with a question mark.
questions.solution:
Split 30 into 5 equal boxes, then take 2 of them:

\[30\div5 = 6\]

\[6\times2 = \boxed{12}\]

\(6\) is only one box; you need 2 of the 5 boxes.

questions.title: Ch 5 Decimals · Ftira and Kinnie
questions.prompt:
At a kiosk a ftira costs €3.40 and a Kinnie costs €1.50.

How much do they cost together?
questions.figure_alt: A ftira with a price tag of €3.40 and a Kinnie with a price tag of €1.50; beside them the column sum 3.40 + 1.50 with a question mark for the total.
questions.solution:
Line up the decimal points:

\[3.40 + 1.50 = \boxed{4.90}\]

- The answer is €4.90.
- \(3.55\) puts the 15 in 1.5 under the cents of 3.40 (\(3.40 + 0.15\)) instead of lining up the decimal points.

questions.title: Ch 5 Decimals · Ten pastizzi
questions.prompt:
One pastizz costs €0.45.

You buy 10 pastizzi, so the cost is \(0.45\times10\) euros.

How much do 10 pastizzi cost?
questions.figure_alt: Ten items of €0.45 each in a row; below, a place-value table with 0.45 in the top row and arrows moving each digit one place left into a row of question marks.
questions.solution:
Every digit moves one place to the left:

\[0.45\times10 = \boxed{4.5}\]

- The cost is €4.50.
- \(0.450\) only adds a zero; the value does not change, so it cannot be ten times bigger.

questions.title: Ch 6 Percentages · Shoe sale
questions.prompt:
Shoes cost €90.

In a sale you get \(10\%\) off (\(10\%\) means 10 out of every 100, the same as one tenth).

How much money do you save?
questions.figure_alt: A bar for €90 cut into 10 equal blocks; the first block (10%) is a question mark.
questions.solution:
\(10\%\) is one block out of 10:

\[90\div10 = \boxed{9}\]

- So \(10\%\) of €90 is €9.
- \(80\) takes 10 away; a percentage is a part, not a subtraction.

questions.title: Ch 6 Percentages · Cinema seats
questions.prompt:
A small cinema has 100 seats in 10 rows of 10.

The red seats are taken.

Per cent means out of 100.

What percentage of the seats is taken?
questions.figure_alt: A 10 by 10 grid of 100 seats: 4 full rows and 5 more are coloured.
questions.solution:
- Per cent means out of 100.
- Count: 4 full rows and 5 more.

\[40 + 5 = 45\]

\[\frac{45}{100} = \boxed{45\%}\]

\(55\%\) counts the empty seats.

questions.title: Ch 7 Ratio · Football cards
questions.prompt:
You and a friend share 18 football cards in the ratio \(1 : 2\).

Your friend gets the bigger share.

How many cards does your friend get?
questions.figure_alt: A bar model: one orange box for you, two blue boxes for a friend, 18 football cards in all; the friend's share is a question mark.
questions.solution:
There are \(1 + 2 = 3\) equal parts:

\[18\div3 = 6\]

\[6\times2 = \boxed{12}\]

6 is the smaller share; 9 splits 18 into 2 halves, but the ratio has 3 parts, not 2.

questions.title: Ch 7 Ratio · Fruit stall
questions.prompt:
A fruit stall has 16 apples and 24 oranges.

Write the ratio apples : oranges, \(16 : 24\), in its simplest form.
questions.figure_alt: Sixteen red counters (apples) in 2 groups of 8 and twenty-four orange counters (oranges) in 3 groups of 8.
questions.solution:
The HCF of 16 and 24 is 8:

\[16\div8 = 2\]

\[24\div8 = 3\]

\[\boxed{2 : 3}\]

- \(4 : 6\) and \(8 : 12\) are the same ratio, but both numbers can still be divided by 2.
- \(3 : 2\) swaps the order: apples come first.

questions.title: Ch 8 Algebra · Parcel on a scale
questions.prompt:
A parcel weighs \(x\) kg.

The parcel and 4 kg of blocks balance 13 kg of blocks, so \(x + 4 = 13\).

Solve to find \(x\).
questions.figure_alt: A balance: a parcel x and 4 one-kilogram blocks on the left, 13 blocks on the right; x is a question mark.
questions.solution:
Take 4 from both sides, so the scale stays balanced:

\[x + 4 = 13\]

\[x = 13 - 4\]

\[x = \boxed{9}\]

17 adds 4 instead of taking it away.

questions.title: Ch 8 Algebra · Taxi fare
questions.prompt:
A taxi charges \(2k + 3\) euros for a trip of \(k\) km.

Here \(2k + 3\) means \(2\times k + 3\).

How many euros is a 6 km trip?
questions.figure_alt: A function machine: 6 km goes in, times 2, plus 3, and the fare in euros is a question mark.
questions.solution:
Put 6 in place of \(k\), multiply first, then add:

\[2\times6 = 12\]

\[12 + 3 = \boxed{15}\]

€29 reads \(2k\) as 26, but \(2k\) means \(2\times k\).

questions.title: Ch 9 Sequences · Matchstick triangles
questions.prompt:
Matchsticks make triangles in a row.

Pattern 1 uses 3 matchsticks, pattern 2 uses 5 and pattern 3 uses 7.

How many matchsticks does pattern 4 use?
questions.figure_alt: Matchstick triangles in a row: 1, 2 and 3 triangles using 3, 5 and 7 sticks; pattern 4 is a question mark.
questions.solution:
Each new pattern adds 2 sticks:

\[7 + 2 = \boxed{9}\]

10 counts 3 sticks for the new triangle, but it shares one side with the triangle before.

questions.title: Ch 9 Sequences · Theatre seats
questions.prompt:
In an open-air theatre, row number \(n\) has \(3n + 2\) seats.

Here \(3n + 2\) means \(3\times n + 2\).

How many seats are in row 10?
questions.figure_alt: A table: rows 1, 2, 3 have 5, 8, 11 seats (each +3); row 10 is a question mark. The rule is 3n + 2.
questions.solution:
Put \(n = 10\) into the rule, multiply first, then add:

\[3\times10 = 30\]

\[30 + 2 = \boxed{32}\]

15 reads \(3n\) as 3 + 10, but \(3n\) means \(3\times n\).

questions.title: Ch 10 Circles · Bicycle wheel
questions.prompt:
A bicycle wheel has radius 35 cm.

Find its diameter.
questions.figure_alt: A bicycle wheel with spokes, a 35 cm radius from the centre and a dashed diameter across it.
questions.solution:
The diameter goes right across, so it is two radii:

\[d = 2r\]

\[d = 2\times35\]

\[d = \boxed{70 \text{ cm}}\]

17.5 cm halves the radius; the diameter is double, not half.

questions.title: Ch 10 Circles · Coin edge
questions.prompt:
A coin has diameter 2 cm.

Use \(\pi \approx 3.14\) to find its circumference (the distance round its edge).
questions.figure_alt: A coin of diameter 2 cm rolled out into a straight line a little more than 3 diameters long.
questions.solution:
The circumference is about 3.14 diameters:

\[C = \pi d\]

\[C \approx 3.14\times2\]

\[C \approx \boxed{6.28 \text{ cm}}\]

3.14 cm uses the radius (1 cm) instead of the diameter, so it is only half way round.

questions.title: Ch 11 Perimeter & Area · Garden lawn
questions.prompt:
A rectangular garden lawn is 9 m long and 5 m wide.

Find its area.
questions.figure_alt: A 9 m by 5 m lawn split into 1 m squares.
questions.solution:
Rows of squares:

\[A = l\times w\]

\[A = 9\times5\]

\[A = \boxed{45 \text{ m}^2}\]

28 m is the perimeter (the distance round), not the area.

questions.title: Ch 11 Perimeter & Area · Festa pennant
questions.prompt:
A festa pennant is a triangle hanging from a string.

Its base (along the string) is 8 cm and its height is 5 cm.

Find its area.
questions.figure_alt: A triangle hanging point-down with base 8 cm along the top and height 5 cm, inside a dashed 8 by 5 rectangle on a grid.
questions.solution:
A triangle is half of its rectangle:

\[A = \tfrac{1}{2}bh\]

\[A = \tfrac{1}{2}\times8\times5\]

\[A = \boxed{20 \text{ cm}^2}\]

40 cm² forgets the half.

questions.title: Ch 12 Surface Area & Nets · Dice
questions.prompt:
A dice is a cube with edges of 3 cm.

Find its surface area.
questions.figure_alt: A cube with 3 cm edges and a net of six squares in a 1–4–1 shape.
questions.solution:
6 square faces, each:

\[\begin{aligned} 3\times3 &= 9 \text{ cm}^2 \\ SA &= 6a^2 \end{aligned}\]

\[SA = 6\times9\]

\[SA = \boxed{54 \text{ cm}^2}\]

27 cm³ is the volume 3 × 3 × 3; surface area covers the outside.

questions.title: Ch 12 Surface Area & Nets · Gift box
questions.prompt:
A gift box is 4 cm long, 3 cm wide and 2 cm high.

Find its volume.
questions.figure_alt: A cuboid 4 by 3 by 2 built from 1 cm cubes.
questions.solution:
Count the cubes, layer by layer:

\[V = lwh\]

\[V = 4\times3\times2\]

\[V = \boxed{24 \text{ cm}^3}\]

9 cm³ adds the three lengths; volume multiplies them.

questions.title: Ch 13 Graphs · Treasure map
questions.prompt:
A treasure map is drawn on a grid.

The treasure chest is buried at point T.

What are the coordinates of T?
questions.figure_alt: A coordinate grid from 0 to 6 across and 0 to 5 up with point T plotted next to a small picture.
questions.solution:
From 0 go 4 across, then 1 up:

\[\boxed{(4, 1)}\]

\((1, 4)\) reads up before across.

questions.title: Ch 13 Graphs · Plant height
questions.prompt:
A sunflower is 3 cm tall and grows 2 cm each week.

Its height is \(y = 2x + 3\) centimetres after \(x\) weeks.

Find \(y\) when \(x = 4\).
questions.figure_alt: The line y = 2x + 3 on a grid; a dashed line from x = 4 goes up to the line at a question mark.
questions.solution:
Put \(x = 4\) into the rule:

\[y = 2\times4 + 3\]

\[y = 8 + 3\]

\[y = \boxed{11}\]

- The answer is 11 cm.
- \(20\) adds \(2 + 3\) first and then multiplies by 4: multiply first.

questions.title: Ch 14 Statistics · Goals scored
questions.prompt:
A football team scored these goals in 7 matches: \(1, 2, 0, 2, 3, 2, 1\).

Find the mode.
questions.figure_alt: A dot plot of 1, 2, 0, 2, 3, 2, 1: the column above 2 is the tallest.
questions.solution:
The mode is the value that appears most often: 2 appears 3 times.

\[\text{mode} = \boxed{2}\]

\(3\) is how many times 2 appears, not the value itself.

questions.title: Ch 14 Statistics · Pages read
questions.prompt:
You read 12, 8, 10 and 14 pages of a book on four days.

Find the mean number of pages per day.
questions.figure_alt: A bar chart of 12, 8, 10, 14; the mean, the level height, is a question mark.
questions.solution:
Add them, then share equally between the 4 values:

\[12 + 8 + 10 + 14 = 44\]

\[44\div4 = \boxed{11}\]

\(44\) is the total; the mean shares it out.

questions.title: Ch 15 Probability · Box of chocolates
questions.prompt:
A box has 3 dark and 7 milk chocolates.

You pick one without looking.

What is the probability that it is dark?
questions.figure_alt: Box of chocolates: 3 dark and 7 milk; the probability is a question mark.
questions.solution:
3 dark out of:

\[\begin{aligned} 3 + 7 &= 10 \\ P(\text{dark}) &= \boxed{\frac{3}{10}} \end{aligned}\]

\(\frac{3}{7}\) compares dark with milk; a probability compares with **all** 10 chocolates.

questions.title: Ch 15 Probability · Not a six
questions.prompt:
You roll a fair dice once.

What is the probability that you do **not** get a 6?
questions.figure_alt: Six dice faces from 1 to 6, the 6 outlined in red.
questions.solution:
\[P(\text{not 6}) = 1 - \frac{1}{6}\]

\[P(\text{not 6}) = \boxed{\frac{5}{6}}\]

- \(\frac{1}{6}\) is P(6) itself.
- \(\frac{6}{5}\) is more than 1, and no probability is more than 1.

questions.title: Ch 16 Constructions · Drinking straws
questions.prompt:
You cut drinking straws to make a triangle.

Which three lengths can make a triangle?
questions.figure_alt: A base of 7 cm with compass arcs of 2 cm and 3 cm from its ends; the arcs leave a gap and never meet.
questions.solution_title: The two short sides must reach
questions.solution:
The two shorter sides together must be longer than the longest:

\[3 + 4 = 7\]

\[7 > 5\]

- So \(\boxed{3 \text{ cm}, 4 \text{ cm}, 5 \text{ cm}}\) works.
- In the others the short sides are too short: \(2 + 3 = 5\), \(1 + 4 = 5\) and \(2 + 5 = 7\), each less than the longest side.

questions.title: Ch 16 Constructions · Pizza slice
questions.prompt:
A slice of pizza has a corner angle of \(80^\circ\).

You cut it in half with a straight cut through the corner.

What is the angle of each smaller slice?
questions.figure_alt: An angle of 80° with a dashed bisector splitting it into two equal angles marked with question marks.
questions.solution:
Bisect means cut into two equal halves:

\[80^\circ\div2 = \boxed{40^\circ}\]

\(160^\circ\) doubles instead of halving.

questions.title: Ch 17 Transformations · Butterfly wing
questions.prompt:
A butterfly picture is symmetric: the \(y\)-axis is its mirror line.

A spot on the right wing is at \((2, 3)\).

Where is the matching spot on the left wing?
questions.figure_alt: A grid with the y-axis as a mirror; the point (2, 3) and a dashed arrow to a question mark on the other side.
questions.solution:
The \(y\)-axis is the mirror: \(x\) changes sign, \(y\) stays.

\[(2, 3) \to \boxed{(-2, 3)}\]

\((2, -3)\) reflects in the \(x\)-axis instead.

questions.title: Ch 17 Transformations · Board game
questions.prompt:
A counter on a board game is at \((1, 1)\).

It moves by \(\binom{3}{2}\): 3 right and 2 up.

Where does it land?
questions.figure_alt: A grid with the point (1, 1), a move of 3 right and 2 up ending at a question mark.
questions.solution:
Add the moves to the coordinates:

\[(1 + 3,\ 1 + 2) = \boxed{(4, 3)}\]

\((3, 2)\) is the move itself, not where the point lands.

questions.title: Ch 18 Real-life Problems · Gozo ferry
questions.prompt:
The Gozo ferry ticket for a car and 2 passengers costs €15.75.

You pay with a €20 note.

How much change do you get?
questions.figure_alt: A receipt with a total of €15.75 next to a €20 note; the change is a question mark.
questions.solution:
Change = money paid − cost:

\[20.00 - 15.75 = \boxed{4.25}\]

- The change is €4.25.
- \(5.75\) takes away only the 15 euros and copies the cents instead of taking them away too.

questions.title: Ch 18 Real-life Problems · Gozo ferry queue
questions.prompt:
You join the queue for the Gozo ferry at 10:45 and drive off in Mġarr at 11:30.

How many minutes does it take?
questions.figure_alt: Two clocks: 10:45 and 11:30, with an arrow between them marked question mark minutes.
questions.solution:
Count up to the hour, then on:

\[10{:}45 \to 11{:}00 = 15 \text{ min}\]

\[11{:}00 \to 11{:}30 = 30 \text{ min}\]

\[15 + 30 = \boxed{45 \text{ min}}\]

\(85\) subtracts 1130 − 1045 as ordinary numbers, but an hour has 60 minutes, not 100.

questions.title: Ch 19 Logo · Hexagon rug
questions.prompt:
A robot vacuum cleans around the edge of a rug shaped like a regular hexagon.

Every inside angle is 120°.

The robot vacuum moves forward 15 steps and turns right, 6 times.

In Logo this is `REPEAT 6 [FD 15 RT ?]`.

- `FD 15` means move forward 15 steps (a length).
- `RT ?` means turn right by ? degrees (an angle).

How many degrees is each turn?
questions.figure_alt: A regular hexagon walked by a robot vacuum that starts facing up: arrows 1 to 6 are forward 15 steps each; one inside angle of 120° is marked; at each corner a dashed straight-on line and a right turn marked with a question mark.
questions.solution:
The robot vacuum turns by how much its direction changes:

- Straight on is a turn of \(0^\circ\).
- Turning round to go back is \(180^\circ\).
- The regular hexagon's inside angle is \(120^\circ\), so the turn is

\[180^\circ - 120^\circ = \boxed{60^\circ}\]

Check: 6 turns make one full spin, \(6\times60^\circ = 360^\circ\), so the robot vacuum ends facing up again.

\(120^\circ\) is the inside angle, not the turn: the turn is measured from the dashed straight-on line.

questions.title: Ch 19 Logo · Hexagon flight
questions.prompt:
A drone flies around a garden shaped like a regular hexagon (every inside angle is 120°).

The drone moves forward 20 steps and turns right at each corner, all the way round.

- `FD 20` means move forward 20 steps (a length).
- `RT` means turn right by that many degrees (an angle).

Which commands draw it?
questions.figure_alt: A regular hexagon walked by a drone that starts facing right: arrows 1 to 6 are forward 20 steps each; one inside angle of 120° is marked; at each corner a dashed straight-on line and a right turn marked with a question mark.
questions.solution:
Count the sides and look at one corner:

- The shape has 6 sides, so the commands repeat \(6\) times.
- Straight on (the dashed line) is a turn of \(0^\circ\).
- Turning round to go back is \(180^\circ\).
- The inside angle is \(120^\circ\), so the turn is

\[180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ\]

Check: \(6\times60^\circ = 360^\circ\), one full spin, so the drone is back at the start, facing right.

\[\boxed{\texttt{REPEAT 6 [FD 20 RT 60]}}\]

`REPEAT 6 [FD 20 RT 120]` uses the inside angle: the drone turns the wrong amount, \(6\times120^\circ = 720^\circ\), so it does not draw a regular hexagon. `REPEAT 6 [FD 20 RT 90]` uses the turn for a square: \(6\times90^\circ = 540^\circ\), not one full spin of \(360^\circ\). `REPEAT 3 [FD 20 RT 60]` repeats only 3 times: \(3\times60^\circ = 180^\circ\), less than a full spin, so the shape does not close.

takeaway:
- Draw it first: a picture shows which rule to use.
- Check that the answer makes sense in the picture.
